content: Hemoglobin C (Hb C) is an abnormal variant of hemoglobin caused by a substitution of glutamic acid with lysine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain (E6K substitution). In individuals who are heterozygous for this mutation, approximately 28–44% of their total hemoglobin is Hb C, and they do not develop anemia. However, in individuals who are homozygous for the mutation, nearly all of their hemoglobin is in the Hb C form, leading to moderate normocytic hemolytic anemia. Individuals who are heterozygous for both Hb C and Hb S (a condition known as Hb SC disease) or for Hb C and thalassemia exhibit atypical hemolytic anemias. In Hb SC disease, the presence of Hb C enhances the sickling of red blood cells. Hemoglobin C is predominantly found in West Africa and has been shown to confer protection against severe malaria. The C designation for Hb C originates from Christchurch, New Zealand, where it was first identified. The clinical significance of Hb C lies in its impact on the plasticity of red blood cells, leading to a hemoglobinopathy. In heterozygous individuals, no anemia develops, while homozygous individuals experience mild hemolytic anemia. In homozygous patients, blood smears reveal target cells, microspherocytes, and Hb C crystals. In individuals with sickle cell–hemoglobin C disease (Hb SC), the gene for Hb S is inherited from one parent, and the gene for Hb C is inherited from the other parent, making them heterozygous. Since Hb C does not polymerize as readily as Hb S, there is less sickling of red blood cells, resulting in fewer sickle cells. Peripheral blood smears in these individuals predominantly show target cells with only a few sickle cells. They also experience fewer acute vaso-occlusive events. However, individuals with Hb SC disease tend to have more severe retinopathy, ischemic necrosis of bone, and priapism compared to those with pure sickle cell disease (Hb SS). The hemoglobin C gene is present in 2–3% of Black individuals in the United States, while 8% of this population carries the hemoglobin S (sickle) gene. Consequently, Hb SC disease is significantly more common than Hb CC disease.
